longread.title: The six Tongan boys who were shipwrecked for 15 months and stayed kind
longread.snippet: In 1965 six runaway schoolboys drifted to an empty island in the South Pacific. When a fisherman found them more than a year later, they had a garden, a fire that never went out, and five songs.
body: In June 1965, six boys slipped out of St Andrew’s, a strict Anglican boarding school in Nukuʻalofa, the capital of Tonga. Their names were Sione Fataua, Stephen (Tevita Fatai Latu), David (Tevita Fifita Siolaʻa), Kolo Fekitoa, Mano (Sione Filipe Totau) and Luke Veikoso. Sources disagree on their ages, but they were teenagers, somewhere between 13 and 19. One of them later said they had sold their school rugby boots and were afraid of what their parents would do. So they did what bored, frightened teenagers sometimes do: they took a boat that was not theirs and set off for adventure. The plan, as far as there was one, was to reach New Zealand.

The boat was about seven metres long, and they left with almost no preparation. On the first night a storm snapped the anchor rope. The wind tore the sail apart and wrecked the rudder. For eight days they drifted southwest, bailing water, with nothing to eat or drink. When the sail went, they tried to keep moving with a blanket. They covered roughly 320 kilometres before someone saw land: a steep, green island ringed by cliffs.

The island was ʻAta, at the far southern end of Tonga. It had once had a village, Kolomaile, with around 350 people. But in 1863 a slaving ship called the Grecian had invited the islanders aboard to trade, locked the hatches once about half of them were below deck, and sailed away. The Tongan king later moved the remaining people to another island for their safety. For a century, ʻAta had belonged to the seabirds.

The boys abandoned their broken boat and swam for the shore, clinging to planks, over something like 36 hours. Mano reached land first. He was too weak to stand, so he called out, and the others followed his voice. They dug a cave with their hands. They ate seabirds and their eggs, and when rain was scarce they drank the birds’ blood.

After about three months they made a two-day climb to the plateau in the old volcanic crater and found the ruins of Kolomaile. Its former residents had left behind a gift: feral chickens, wild taro and bananas, the descendants of an abandoned village’s gardens. The boys moved up there and began, in effect, to run a small community.

They split the work into pairs: garden duty, kitchen duty, guard duty. They hollowed out tree trunks to catch rainwater. Stephen, who would later become an engineer, got a fire going by rubbing two sticks together, and they kept that fire alive for more than a year. At night they sang. Someone built a makeshift guitar, and over those months they composed five songs. Once they built a raft and tried to escape, but it broke apart about a kilometre and a half offshore and they had to struggle back. They thought they were close to Samoa, which meant that any successful escape would have sent them straight into the open ocean.

On 11 September 1966, an Australian lobster fisherman named Peter Warner was sailing his boat, the Just David, home past ʻAta. He noticed patches of burned grass on the cliffs, which is an odd thing to see on an island that is supposed to be empty. Warner had heard that dangerous criminals were sometimes marooned on remote islands, so he approached carefully. Then a boy swam out to the boat. It was Stephen, and he explained everything in English. Mano remembered later that the crew were terrified at first, because the boys were all naked, with long hair.

Warner radioed the boys’ names to Nukuʻalofa and waited about twenty minutes. The reply, as Wikipedia records it, was that the boys had been given up for dead and their funerals had already been held. If it really was them, the radio operator said, it was a miracle.

All six were found to be healthy. Their families threw enormous celebrations. Then came a comic twist. When the boys failed to turn up at a party Warner was giving for them, he found out they had been arrested, because the owner of the boat had pressed charges. Warner sold the rights to their story to Sydney’s Channel 7 and used £150 from the deal to pay the owner, who dropped the case. A television crew took the boys back to ʻAta to film a re-enactment called The Castaways, broadcast in October 1966. Warner then hired the six as crew for a lobster boat. Their families taught him where to find Pacific spiny lobster, and he received a royal concession to trap them in Tongan waters.

For decades the story lived mainly in Tonga, where it was never really forgotten. In 2015 the Spanish explorer Álvaro Cerezo spent ten days on ʻAta with Kolo Fekitoa, by then in his sixties. In 2020 the Dutch historian Rutger Bregman made the boys famous worldwide in his book Humankind, presenting them as a real-life answer to William Golding’s Lord of the Flies, the novel in which stranded schoolboys descend into savagery. Some Tongan writers have pushed back on that framing, pointing out that the boys were not a Western thought experiment but Tongan teenagers raised in a culture of shared work and faith. Either way, the outcome is the same.

In 2020, one of the survivors, Tevita Siolaʻa, told New Zealand’s 1News that four of the six were still alive, and that the film rights had been sold to New Regency, with any proceeds to be shared equally. It is a pleasing ending for a story that began with six scared kids, a stolen boat, and a fire that two sticks and a lot of patience kept burning for fifteen months.

items.title: Nevada’s rainbow Fly Geyser was created by accident by a botched well
items.snippet: A failed geothermal well from 1964 built one of the strangest landscapes in the American West, and it now belongs to Burning Man.
body: In the desert of northern Nevada, near the Black Rock Desert, a cluster of lumpy mineral cones sprays near-boiling water into the air, surrounded by terraced pools. The cones are streaked green and red. It looks like something from another planet. It is actually the result of two wells that went wrong.

In 1916, a farmer drilling for irrigation water hit scalding geothermal water instead, and the well was abandoned. In 1964, a geothermal company drilled another well nearby, found the water was not hot enough to be useful, and left it uncapped. The water has been escaping ever since, leaving minerals behind that slowly built the cones. The colours come from heat-loving microorganisms living in the water.
more: Fly Geyser, also called Fly Ranch Geyser, sits on private land in Washoe County, Nevada, a little north of the tiny town of Gerlach, near Fly Reservoir in an area called Hualapai Flat. It is just west of the Black Rock Desert, the dry lakebed best known as the home of the Burning Man festival.

The geyser is a rare example of a landmark built by a mistake. The first well, drilled in 1916 to find water for irrigation, struck geothermal water close to boiling point, which is no good for crops, and it was abandoned. Nearly fifty years later, in 1964, a geothermal energy company drilled a second well nearby, hoping to use that heat. The water turned out not to be hot enough for power generation, and the company walked away without properly sealing it.

The 1964 well never stopped flowing. Its uncontrolled discharge also caused the original 1916 geyser to dry up. As the hot water spills out, it carries dissolved minerals, and as it cools those minerals settle out and harden. Over the decades they have built up a set of cones and mounds, plus travertine terraces and dozens of pools spread across a wide area. The water reaches about 93 °C and erupts roughly a metre and a half into the air.

The striking colours are alive. Thermophilic, or heat-loving, microorganisms thrive in the warm, wet surfaces and paint the rock in greens and reds. Different organisms prefer different temperatures, which is why the colour changes across the mound and around the pools.

For years the geyser was mostly known from photographs, because it sits on a private ranch. In June 2016 the nonprofit Burning Man Project bought the whole Fly Ranch, about 3,800 acres including the geyser, for 6.5 million dollars. It began allowing limited public access in May 2018.

Today you can visit on small guided nature walks of about three hours, which run from April to October. The tours are organised by the Friends of Black Rock High Rock, a local conservation group, and the ticket price counts as a donation that supports the ranch and the group.

Measurements of the site vary a little between sources, including the exact distance from Gerlach and the height of the mound, so treat any precise figures with some caution. What everyone agrees on is the basic story: two abandoned wells, decades of mineral-rich water and a landscape nobody planned.
It is a nice reminder that not every wonder of nature is entirely natural. Sometimes it is just nature quietly making something beautiful out of a hole that people forgot to close.

items.title: Robert Smalls escaped slavery by stealing a Confederate warship at 3 a.m.
items.snippet: Dressed as the captain, he steamed past five forts, including Fort Sumter, and handed the ship to the Union Navy. Later he served in Congress.
body: On the night of 12 May 1862, the three white officers of the Confederate steamer Planter went ashore in Charleston, leaving the enslaved crew on board. Robert Smalls, the ship’s pilot, had been waiting for exactly that.

At about 3 a.m. he took the ship out, stopped at another wharf to pick up his wife, children and other family members, and headed for the harbour mouth. He wore the captain’s uniform and a straw hat like his, copied his posture, and gave the correct whistle signals at each checkpoint. He passed five Confederate forts, including Fort Sumter, at an unhurried pace. Out of range, he raised a white bed sheet and surrendered the ship to the Union fleet. He later served five terms in the US Congress.
more: Robert Smalls was born into slavery in Beaufort, South Carolina, and by 1862 he was working as a skilled pilot on the CSS Planter, a Confederate transport steamer in Charleston harbour. Pilots needed to know the channels, the signals and the routines of the harbour, and Smalls knew them all.

On 12 May 1862, the Planter loaded four large guns at Coles Island and about 200 pounds of ammunition and firewood in Charleston. That evening, the three white officers went ashore for the night. Smalls and seven of the eight enslaved crewmen stayed aboard and put their plan into motion. Some of the men had arranged for their families to hide on another steamer at the North Atlantic wharf.

At about 3 a.m. on 13 May, Smalls took the ship away from the wharf and stopped to collect the families, including his wife Hannah and their children. He put on the captain’s uniform and a straw hat that resembled Captain Charles Relyea’s, and he imitated the captain’s manner on deck, so that anyone watching from shore would see a familiar silhouette.

Then came the frightening part. Charleston harbour was guarded by five Confederate forts. At each checkpoint, Smalls gave the correct steam-whistle signals. When Fort Sumter challenged the ship at around 4:30 a.m., he answered with the right hand signals. He deliberately kept a normal, steady course rather than racing for the exit, reasoning that a ship in a hurry would draw attention.

Once the Planter was out of range of the guns, he turned towards the Union blockade fleet and raised a white bed sheet that his wife had brought aboard. Even so, the USS Onward nearly opened fire before a crewman spotted the flag. The Onward’s captain, John Frederick Nickels, came aboard, and Smalls asked for a US flag and formally handed over the ship and its cargo.
Congress awarded prize money to Smalls and his crew. He received 1,500 dollars in 1862, and in 1900 Congress paid him a further sum, though many felt it was still less than he deserved.

His life after the war was as remarkable as the escape. He served in the South Carolina House of Representatives from 1868 and in the state Senate from 1870 to 1875. He was then elected to the US House of Representatives, serving from 1875 to 1879, again in 1882 and 1883, and from 1884 to 1887.

There is a beautiful detail at the centre of his later life. After the war, he bought the house at 511 Prince Street in Beaufort, the house where he had been born enslaved. When the former owner sued to get it back, Smalls kept it, and the case became a precedent in similar disputes. He died there, in Beaufort, in 1915, at the age of 75.

items.title: TIL a stewardess survived the Olympic crash, the Titanic and the Britannic
items.snippet: Violet Jessop was on board all three White Star sister ships when disaster struck, and she lived to 83.
body: Violet Jessop worked as a stewardess and nurse on ocean liners, and she has the strangest CV at sea. She was on board the RMS Olympic when it collided with the warship HMS Hawke in 1911. She was on the Titanic when it sank in April 1912. And in 1916, while serving as a wartime nurse, she was on HMHS Britannic, the third sister ship, when it hit a German mine in the Aegean and sank in 55 minutes.

She survived all three. On the Titanic she was put in lifeboat 16 and handed a baby to hold. On the Britannic she jumped out of her lifeboat to escape the ship’s propellers and hit her head, but recovered. Then she went straight back to sea for decades. People called her Miss Unsinkable.
more: Jessop was born in 1887 near Bahía Blanca, Argentina, to Irish immigrants. As a child she survived tuberculosis that doctors expected to kill her, which in hindsight looks like a warm-up. After her father died, the family moved to England, and at 21 she became a stewardess, starting with the Royal Mail Line in 1908.

Her first brush with disaster came on 20 September 1911. The Olympic, the first of White Star Line’s three giant Olympic-class liners, had just left Southampton when it collided with the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Hawke. Nobody died, and the ship limped back to port. Jessop did not even mention it in her memoirs, which tells you something about how the rest of her career went.

She joined the Titanic on 10 April 1912. After the ship struck the iceberg on the night of 14 April, she was ordered up on deck to set an example for passengers who did not speak English, showing them what to do. She was placed in lifeboat 16, and as it was lowered, Sixth Officer James Moody handed her a baby to look after. The survivors were picked up by the Carpathia and reached New York on 18 April.

There is a lovely but shaky coda to the baby story. Jessop later said a woman phoned her years afterwards to tell her, “I was that baby.” Her co-author, the historian John Maxtone-Graham, thought the call was probably a prank. The only baby recorded in lifeboat 16, As’ad Tannūs, died in 1931.

During the First World War, Jessop served as a nurse with the Voluntary Aid Detachment. On 21 November 1916 she was aboard HMHS Britannic, the third sister, which had been converted into a hospital ship. It struck a German mine in the Aegean Sea and sank in 55 minutes. Of the 1,066 people aboard, 30 died, many of them in lifeboats sucked into the ship’s still-turning propellers. Jessop jumped from her lifeboat to get away, struck her head, and recovered.

Remarkably, none of this put her off. She returned to White Star Line in 1920, moved to the Red Star Line, sailed around the world twice on the Belgenland, and later went back to the Royal Mail Line. She married a fellow steward, John James Lewis, in 1923; they divorced about a year later. In 1950 she retired to the village of Great Ashfield in Suffolk.

She died of heart failure on 5 May 1971, at 83. Her memoir was published in 1997 as Titanic Survivor, edited with Maxtone-Graham. In 2006, the diver Rosemary Lunn re-enacted her Britannic jump during an expedition to the wreck, which is either a beautiful tribute or a sign that some people simply love the sea too much.

items.title: 7 famous discoveries named after the wrong person (including the law itself)
items.snippet: Stigler’s law says no scientific discovery is named after whoever found it first. Fittingly, Stigler didn’t come up with it.
body: In 1980 the University of Chicago statistician Stephen Stigler proposed a rule: no scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer. Names tend to go to whoever popularised an idea, not whoever had it first.
The best part: Stigler credited the insight to the sociologist Robert K. Merton. So Stigler’s law is itself an example of Stigler’s law.

Once you start looking, it is everywhere. Halley’s Comet had been observed since at least 240 BC. Halley just worked out its orbit and predicted its return. The Fibonacci sequence appears in Indian mathematics around 200 BC, about 1,400 years before Fibonacci wrote it down in 1202. The bell curve is called the Gaussian distribution, but Abraham de Moivre described it in 1733, decades before Gauss began using it. And Hubble’s law was derived by Georges Lemaître two years before Edwin Hubble.
more: Stigler published his idea in a collection of essays honouring Robert K. Merton, the sociologist who had studied how credit works in science. Stigler simply gave the eponym problem a catchy formulation, and then politely handed the credit back to Merton, which is the most elegant joke in the history of statistics.
Here is a short list of repeat offenders, taken from Wikipedia’s long list of examples.

1. Halley’s Comet. Astronomers recorded it since at least 240 BC. Edmond Halley’s achievement was different and real: he calculated its orbit and correctly predicted when it would come back. The name rewards the prediction, not the discovery.
2. The Fibonacci numbers. The sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on was known in Indian mathematics around 200 BC. Leonardo of Pisa, later called Fibonacci, introduced it to European readers in 1202.
3. The Gaussian distribution. The famous bell curve was introduced by Abraham de Moivre in 1733. Carl Friedrich Gauss started using it in 1794, and his name stuck.

4. The Poisson distribution. Siméon Denis Poisson described it in 1837. De Moivre, again, had already given the result between 1711 and 1721. If there is a patron saint of uncredited mathematicians, it is probably him.

5. Hubble’s law. The relationship between a galaxy’s distance and how fast it moves away from us was derived by the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître two years before Edwin Hubble published it.
6. Benford’s law. The odd fact that, in many real-world data sets, the leading digit is far more likely to be 1 than 9 was stated by Frank Benford in 1938. Simon Newcomb had noticed it in 1881.

7. The Vigenère cipher. The classic polyalphabetic cipher was described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in a book in 1553. In the 19th century it was misattributed to Blaise de Vigenère, and the wrong name never left.

There are others. The von Neumann architecture, the basic design of most computers, carries John von Neumann’s name because of a draft report he wrote on the EDVAC computer, which left out the names of its inventors, John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert. The Bessemer process for making steel was discovered by William Kelly in 1851, but Henry Bessemer patented it first, in 1855. And the Pythagorean theorem was known to Babylonian mathematicians long before Pythagoras; nobody even knows whether Pythagoras proved it.

None of this means the famous names were frauds. Halley really did predict a comet. Gauss really was a genius. But the law is a good reminder that knowledge is usually a relay race, and the person holding the baton when the crowd starts cheering is not always the one who started running.

items.title: In 1518, Strasbourg caught a plague of dancing and hired a band to cure it
items.snippet: One woman started dancing in the street and couldn’t stop. Within weeks dozens, maybe hundreds, joined her.
body: On 14 July 1518, a woman known as Frau Troffea began dancing in a street in Strasbourg, then part of the Holy Roman Empire. She reportedly kept going for about a week, stopping only to sleep. Others joined, including her husband. Within days, more than thirty people were dancing. By August, estimates ranged from 50 to 400.

The city’s response was memorable. Doctors advised that the dancers should dance it out, so the council hired musicians and strong men to keep people on their feet and opened guild halls for them. It made things worse. The council then banned public music and dancing and sent the afflicted to a shrine of Saint Vitus. By September, it was over. Historians still argue about why it happened.
more: The dancing plague of 1518 ran from July to September in Strasbourg, a city now in France. It began with one woman, recorded as Frau Troffea, who started dancing in the street on 14 July and seemingly could not stop. Over the following days and weeks, more people were swept up. Accounts describe dancers collapsing from exhaustion, hunger and thirst, and some reportedly danced until their feet bled into their shoes.

What makes the episode so strange is not only the dancing but the official reaction. Local physicians, working with the medical ideas of the time, blamed “overheated blood.” The cure for overheated blood, they believed, was more dancing followed by rest. So the city council did something that sounds like satire: it hired musicians and strong men to support the dancers and keep them moving, and it refurbished guild halls to give them space.

It backfired. More people joined in. The council changed course, banned public dancing and music, and turned to religion instead. Many people believed the dancers had been cursed by Saint Vitus. The afflicted were taken to a shrine dedicated to him, where they were given red shoes sprinkled with holy water, small crosses to carry, incense and Latin incantations. By September, the remaining dancers were led to a chapel on a mountaintop to pray for absolution, and the outbreak ended.

How many people died is a genuinely open question. Some popular accounts claim that up to fifteen people a day died at the peak. But, as the Wikipedia article points out, Strasbourg’s contemporary sources do not mention deaths at all. The main modern source for the death toll is the historian John Waller, and the accounts he cites date from later periods. The honest answer is that nobody knows.
Theories about the cause have come and gone. One idea is ergot poisoning: a fungus that grows on damp rye and can cause convulsions and hallucinations. Waller, however, argues that it is unlikely.

Waller’s preferred explanation, and the most popular one today, is a mass psychogenic illness, a kind of stress-induced collective behaviour. The region had been suffering famine, disease and hardship, and people strongly believed in the power of saints to curse and to heal. In that atmosphere, he argues, the idea of being compelled to dance could spread from person to person like a real disease.

At the time, people offered their own explanations: demonic possession, divine punishment or bad blood. Today we have different vocabulary, but the dancing plague remains one of history’s oddest reminders of how strongly belief, fear and crowds can shape what bodies do.

items.title: TIL a Syrian brown bear was enlisted in the Polish army and made corporal
items.snippet: Wojtek was adopted as a cub in Iran in 1942, given a service number to get past a no-pets rule, and later retired to Edinburgh Zoo.
body: In April 1942, Polish soldiers passing through Iran met a local boy with a bear cub. One of their officers bought it, and the cub ended up with a transport unit that became the 22nd Artillery Supply Company of the 2nd Polish Corps. They named him Wojtek.

There was a problem: British transport ships did not allow pets. So the soldiers enlisted Wojtek as a private, with his own service number. He was later promoted to corporal. He wrestled with the men, learned to salute, and walked on his hind legs to copy them. He grew to about 500 kg, and after the war he lived at Edinburgh Zoo until 1963. Statues of him stand in Edinburgh, Kraków and several other cities.
more: Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear, and his life is one of the more charming footnotes of the Second World War. In April 1942, near Hamadan in Iran, Polish soldiers came across an Iranian boy with a cub. Accounts differ about exactly how the bear changed hands, but Lieutenant Anatol Tarnowiecki bought it, and for a while a Polish refugee, Irena Bokiewicz, looked after it.

In August 1942 the cub was handed over to a transport company that later became the 22nd Artillery Supply Company of the 2nd Polish Corps. The soldiers called him Wojtek. At first he was fed condensed milk from an old vodka bottle. As he grew, he developed a taste for fruit, honey and beer, and he is often said to have smoked and drunk coffee, though fact-checkers have pointed out that eating a cigarette is more likely than smoking one.

He became part of the unit’s daily life. He wrestled with the soldiers, learned to salute, and walked upright, apparently imitating the men around him. When the corps needed to be shipped onwards, British rules banned animals on troop transports. The solution was wonderfully bureaucratic: Wojtek was officially enlisted as a private, with a service number. He was later promoted to corporal.

The most famous Wojtek story is that during the Battle of Monte Cassino in Italy in 1944, he helped carry crates of 25-pounder artillery shells. The tale is widely repeated, but Wikipedia notes that it is debated. What is not debated is that his unit adopted an emblem showing a bear carrying an artillery shell.
After he was demobilised in 1947, Wojtek went to Edinburgh Zoo. He lived there for the rest of his life and died on 2 December 1963, aged 21, weighing about 500 kg.

Part of his charm is that the soldiers treated him as one of their own. He was not a mascot kept in a cage at the back of the camp but a member of the company, fed, teased, wrestled with and, on paper at least, entitled to his rations like any other soldier.

He has not been forgotten. Statues of Wojtek stand in Edinburgh, Kraków, Duns, Cassino, Szczecin, Poznań and Sopot. In 2023 an animated short, A Bear Named Wojtek, collected a series of award nominations and made the Academy Award shortlist.

It is a story that is easy to love because it is half war history and half wholesome absurdity: a group of displaced soldiers, far from home, found a small creature to look after, and then bent the rules of the British Army to keep him.

items.title: TIL a park ranger was struck by lightning seven times and survived them all
items.snippet: Roy Sullivan of Shenandoah National Park holds the Guinness record. The last strike came while he was fishing, and then a bear showed up.
body: Roy Sullivan worked as a ranger in Shenandoah National Park in Virginia from 1936. Guinness World Records recognises him as the person struck by lightning more times than anyone else: seven, between 1942 and 1977.

The details read like a running joke. In 1942 he was hit in a fire lookout tower with no lightning rod. In 1969 a bolt came through his truck window and burned off his eyebrows. In 1972 his hair caught fire inside a ranger station. In 1973 he stepped out of his truck to escape a storm cloud he felt was following him, and got hit anyway. The seventh strike, in 1977, came while he was fishing. Afterwards a bear tried to steal his trout, and he fought it off with a branch.
more: Roy Cleveland Sullivan was born in 1912 in Greene County, Virginia, and joined Shenandoah National Park as a ranger in 1936. He was described as brawny, with a rugged face reminiscent of the actor Gene Hackman. He would become famous for something far less pleasant than his looks.

Strike one came in April 1942, in a newly built fire lookout tower that did not yet have a lightning rod. He later said that fire was jumping all over the place. He came away with a burn along his right leg and a hole in his shoe.

Strike two, July 1969: he was driving on a mountain road when lightning hit nearby trees and the bolt came in through the open window. He was knocked unconscious, his eyebrows and eyelashes were burned off, and his hair caught fire. The truck rolled on until it stopped near the edge of a cliff.

Strike three, July 1970: he was in his front yard when lightning hit a power transformer and jumped to his left shoulder. Strike four, spring 1972: he was inside a ranger station, and his hair caught fire again. He tried to put his head under the tap in the restroom, could not fit, and used a wet towel.

Strike five, 7 August 1973, is the one that made him sound cursed. While on patrol he saw a storm cloud and drove away from it, feeling it was following him. When he thought he had escaped, he got out of the truck and was struck. The bolt ran down his left arm and leg and knocked off a shoe. Still conscious, he poured a can of water over his burning head. Strike six, in June 1976, came when another cloud he believed was following him caught up; he hurt an ankle and, yes, his hair caught fire.

Strike seven, 25 June 1977, happened while he was fishing in a freshwater pool. The bolt hit the top of his head and burned his chest and stomach. Then a bear tried to steal the trout from his line, and he hit it with a branch.

His wife was struck once too, while hanging laundry; he was beside her and unharmed. People began to avoid him in his later years, worried about standing next to him in a storm, which reportedly saddened him.

A note of caution: all seven strikes were documented by the park superintendent, R. Taylor Hoskins, who was not actually present at any of them. Still, Guinness accepts the record, and two of Sullivan’s scorched ranger hats ended up on display in Guinness exhibition halls. He died in 1983, aged 71.

items.title: B.F. Skinner built a missile steered by pigeons pecking at a screen
items.snippet: Project Pigeon actually worked in tests, got 25,000 dollars in wartime funding, and won its inventor an Ig Nobel Prize 80 years later.
body: During the Second World War, the psychologist B.F. Skinner, famous for his studies of how rewards shape behaviour, proposed a guided bomb with an unusual navigation system: pigeons.

Lenses in the nose of the bomb projected an image of the target onto a screen. One to three trained pigeons inside pecked at the target’s image. If the image drifted off-centre, their pecking tilted the screen, and sensors turned that into steering commands. When three birds disagreed, the majority won.

The military thought it was eccentric but gave it 25,000 dollars. It was cancelled in 1944, briefly revived by the Navy as Project Orcon, and finally killed in 1953 when electronic guidance became reliable. In 2024 Skinner was posthumously awarded the Ig Nobel Peace Prize for it.
more: Burrhus Frederic Skinner is one of the most influential psychologists of the 20th century, best known for operant conditioning: the idea that behaviour can be shaped by rewarding the right actions. During the war, he looked at the problem of guiding a bomb onto a target and saw a bird-shaped solution.

The airframe for Project Pigeon was an unpowered glider developed by the US National Bureau of Standards, the same design the Navy later used for its radar-guided Bat glide bomb. In the nose, three lenses projected an image of what lay ahead onto a pivoting screen. Inside sat the guidance system: one, two or three pigeons, each trained to peck at the image of the target.

As long as the target stayed in the middle, nothing happened. If it drifted towards the edge of the screen, the birds’ pecking followed it, which moved the screen. Sensors detected that movement and sent signals to the control surfaces to steer the bomb back on course. With three birds, the system followed the majority, and a pigeon that disagreed with its colleagues was punished. Somewhere in there is a lesson about committee meetings.

The training was impressive. Skinner rewarded the birds with food for pecking faster and more accurately. One pigeon reportedly pecked more than 10,000 times in 45 minutes. In his laboratory demonstrations, the birds really could keep a target centred.

The National Defense Research Committee was sceptical. It considered the idea eccentric and impractical, but contributed 25,000 dollars anyway. On 8 October 1944, the programme was cancelled because the military judged other projects more promising for actual combat.

The pigeons got a second chance. In 1948 the US Navy revived the idea under the much more serious-sounding name Project Orcon, short for organic control. It lasted until 1953, when electronic guidance systems finally became reliable enough to make birds unnecessary.

Skinner’s pigeons had one more moment in the spotlight. In 2024, decades after his death, Skinner was awarded the Ig Nobel Peace Prize for Project Pigeon. The Ig Nobels honour research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think. His daughter, Julie Vargas, accepted the award on his behalf.

It is easy to laugh, but the underlying idea was clever: at a time when there were no computers small enough to recognise a target, a pigeon’s brain was the most compact image processor available. The machines simply caught up.

items.title: Boring, Oregon is twinned with Dull, Scotland, and later Bland, Australia joined in
items.snippet: A Scottish cyclist rode through Boring in 2011 and had an idea. Now three towns form the League of Extraordinary Communities.
body: Boring is a community of about 8,000 people near Portland, Oregon. It is named after William Harrison Boring, a Union veteran who farmed there in the 1870s, not after the local nightlife.

In 2011, Elizabeth Leighton from Aberfeldy, Scotland, passed through Boring on a cycling holiday and realised it had a natural partner back home: the tiny village of Dull, population 84. She proposed a pairing, and in June 2012 Boring accepted. The two places now promote tourism together, with commemorative T-shirts and mugs reading “Boring & Dull: a pair for the ages.”
In 2013, Bland Shire in New South Wales, Australia, joined. Together they call themselves the League of Extraordinary Communities.
more: Boring, in Clackamas County, Oregon, is an unincorporated community whose name has launched a thousand jokes. It comes from William Harrison Boring, an Illinois native who fought for the Union at the Siege of Vicksburg and then moved west. His half-brother Joseph settled in the area in 1856; William started farming there in 1874 and later donated land for the community’s first schoolhouse.

For a long time the name was just a mild burden. Then a Scottish visitor turned it into an asset. In 2011, Elizabeth Leighton, from Aberfeldy in Perthshire, was on a cycling holiday in Oregon and rode through Boring. Near her home was a hamlet called Dull, with just 84 residents. The idea of a partnership practically wrote itself.

Boring formally accepted the pairing in June 2012. The idea was always tongue-in-cheek, but it was also smart tourism: two small places that most travellers would never think of suddenly had a reason to be visited and photographed. The Boring Community Planning Organisation issued T-shirts and mugs for the occasion, and Time magazine ran a piece in August 2013 titled “Happy Boring & Dull Day!”

That same year, a third member joined. Bland Shire, a local government area in New South Wales, Australia, signed up, and the three places now describe themselves as the League of Extraordinary Communities, promoting travel to all of them. The name is the best part: it takes three words that sound like insults and turns them into a club.

Boring has some genuine claims to interest of its own. The nearby Boring Lava Field, a group of about 80 small volcanic vents, is named after the town. The Springwater Corridor, a popular rail trail for walkers and cyclists, starts there and follows an old railway line. And the creators of Disney’s animated series Gravity Falls have said the show’s fictional small town was inspired by Boring.

According to the 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey, the Boring area has around 8,300 residents, roughly a hundred times the population of Dull. It is an uneven partnership on paper, but a very even one in terms of jokes.

Supporters of a bid to turn Boring into an official village even adopted the slogan “The most exciting place to live.” The bid failed, in a 2006 referendum, by just five votes: 293 to 298. Which, if you think about it, is a genuinely exciting result.

For a cyclist, there is something especially pleasing in the origin story. One person on a bike holiday noticed a funny sign, remembered a funny village at home, and ended up connecting communities on three continents.

items.title: London Bridge is in the Arizona desert, and the buyer didn’t mistake it for Tower Bridge
items.snippet: In 1968 an American developer bought the old London Bridge, shipped its stones through the Panama Canal and rebuilt it over a lake in Arizona.
body: By the 1960s, the 19th-century London Bridge over the Thames was too weak for modern traffic, so the City of London put it up for sale. In April 1968 it was bought for £1.02 million by Robert McCulloch, an entrepreneur who had founded a new town called Lake Havasu City in Arizona.

Workers numbered the facing stones and recorded where each one went. The stones were shipped through the Panama Canal to California, trucked to Arizona, and used to clad a new concrete bridge. It reopened on 10 October 1971.

There is a famous story that McCulloch thought he was buying the much grander Tower Bridge. Both he and Ivan Luckin, who arranged the sale, denied it. The bridge worked as intended: it pulled in visitors and helped sell land.
more: The London Bridge that now stands in Lake Havasu City spent the 19th century and much of the 20th crossing the Thames. By the 1960s it was judged too weak for heavy modern traffic, so the City of London decided to replace it. Rather than simply demolishing it, the City put it on the market.

The buyer was Robert P. McCulloch, an entrepreneur who was developing a brand new town in the Arizona desert beside Lake Havasu, a reservoir on the Colorado River. In April 1968 he paid £1.02 million, about 2.46 million dollars at the time. He needed something to make people come and look at his land. A famous bridge would do the trick.

Moving a bridge across the world is not a simple job. The facing stones were removed, numbered and catalogued so that each could go back in its original position. They were taken to a quarry at Merrivale in Devon, where many were sliced thinner, by 15 to 20 centimetres, to make them lighter. A newly built cargo ship carried them through the Panama Canal to Long Beach, California, and from there they travelled by truck to Arizona. The deal was cheap: McCulloch’s real estate agent paid the voyage’s operating costs in exchange for the cargo.

In Arizona, the bridge was not rebuilt stone by stone in the old way. Instead, a modern concrete structure was built and clad in the original granite. The foundation stone was re-laid on 23 September 1968. Sundt Construction finished the job in late 1971, and the bridge was rededicated on 10 October 1971.

And then there is the legend. For decades, people have told the story that McCulloch thought he was buying Tower Bridge, the ornate one with the towers that everyone pictures when they think of London, and only realised his mistake when the plain arches arrived. It is a great story, but both McCulloch and Ivan Luckin, the man who arranged the sale, denied it.

Whatever its origins, the plan worked. Tours of the bridge brought people to Lake Havasu City, many of them stayed long enough to look at land for sale, and McCulloch recouped what he had spent. Today it is one of Arizona’s best-known attractions, a slightly surreal sight of a Victorian London bridge among palm trees and speedboats.
It also makes for one of the best pub quiz answers in existence. Where is London Bridge? Arizona. Mostly.

items.title: The Wilhelm scream: a 1951 alligator-attack yelp heard in over 400 films
items.snippet: Recorded for a forgotten western, rescued by Star Wars sound designer Ben Burtt, and now free for anyone to use.
body: If you have watched enough action films, you have heard it: a short, strangled scream when someone falls or gets shot. It is called the Wilhelm scream, and it is one recording reused for more than 70 years.

It was recorded for the 1951 western Distant Drums, for a scene where a soldier is dragged underwater by an alligator. The reel was labelled “Man getting bit by an alligator, and he screams.” The voice is believed to be Sheb Wooley, later famous for the song The Purple People Eater.

Sound designer Ben Burtt found it in a studio archive and used it in Star Wars in 1977, when Luke shoots a stormtrooper off a ledge. He named it after Private Wilhelm, a minor character who screams it in a 1953 film. Since then it has turned up in more than 400 films.
more: The Wilhelm scream started life as an ordinary studio sound effect. For the 1951 Warner Bros. film Distant Drums, a set of screams was recorded in a single session, labelled “Man getting bit by an alligator, and he screams.” There were at least six takes. The fifth was used for the swamp scene where a soldier is pulled under by an alligator; the fourth is the one we now call the Wilhelm scream, and it was used three other times in the same film.

Who is screaming? There is no definitive answer, but the best evidence points to Sheb Wooley, an actor and singer who had a small, uncredited role in Distant Drums and who is best remembered for the 1958 novelty hit The Purple People Eater and for the TV series Rawhide. Ben Burtt found Warner Bros. records listing the actors scheduled to record extra vocals for the film, and Wooley was one of them. In 2005 his widow, Linda Dotson, said he used to joke about how good he was at screaming and dying in films.

Because sound effects were expensive, Warner Bros. reused the scream in other productions throughout the 1950s, including Springfield Rifle, Them!, A Star Is Born, Land of the Pharaohs and The Charge at Feather River (1953). In that last film, a character called Private Wilhelm lets out the scream after being shot in the thigh with an arrow. That is where the name comes from.

For a couple of decades the recording sat quietly in the archive. Then, in the 1970s, a young sound designer named Ben Burtt came across it on an old studio reel. He used it in Star Wars in 1977, when Luke Skywalker shoots a stormtrooper who falls from a ledge, and nicknamed it after Private Wilhelm. Burtt turned it into a personal signature, slipping it into every Indiana Jones film, Lucas-era Star Wars films, and other projects such as Willow and Gremlins.

Burtt kept using it, in films from Anchorman to Die Hard with a Vengeance, Lethal Weapon 4 and The Fifth Element, and it spread well beyond his own work. The National Science and Media Museum in the UK has said it has appeared in more than 400 films. For viewers who know to listen for it, it has become a kind of in-joke.
Not everyone kept using it. In February 2018 Lucasfilm said the Star Wars films would stop including the scream, making The Force Awakens (2015) the last of them to feature it.

Here is the nicest twist for anyone who edits video. The original sound collection, the Sunset Editorial library, was donated to the USC School of Cinematic Arts in 1990. In 2023, on USC’s behalf, Craig Smith released the full original recording session on Freesound under a CC0 licence, meaning it is effectively in the public domain. The collection was also mirrored on the Internet Archive. So if you have ever wanted the real Wilhelm scream for your own timeline, it is free.

items.title: A shark has refused to leave a Busan canal for a month and 1.5 million came to see it
items.snippet: Nicknamed Bukangi, the three-metre shark has beaten two Coast Guard rescue attempts and turned a quiet park into Busan’s hottest attraction.
body: On 18 September, a three-metre shark turned up in a narrow artificial canal at Busan North Port Waterfront Park in South Korea. A month later, it is still there, and it seems to like it.

Locals nicknamed it Bukangi, after Bukhang, the North Port. The Coast Guard tried twice to guide it back to the sea, first with water jets and then with a large custom net. In the second attempt they got it within 100 metres of the exit. The next day it swam over the net and went back in. Rescue efforts are now suspended.

Officials say the shark is in good health and has plenty of mullet and mackerel to eat. The park used to get about 2,000 visitors on a weekend. Since Bukangi arrived, more than 1.5 million people have come to watch it swim laps at about 5 km/h.
more: The story of Bukangi has become one of South Korea’s happiest small news sagas of the autumn. The shark, described by the Asia Business Daily as a three-metre black shark, was first spotted on 18 September in an artificial canal connected to the sea at North Port Waterfront Park in Busan’s Dong-gu district. Its exact species has not been officially confirmed, and different outlets have described it slightly differently.

From the start, it showed no interest in leaving. Maritime police tried to drive it out and gave up. On 29 September, five Coast Guard and related vessels sprayed jets of water to herd it towards open water; according to the Korea Times, it kept dodging, and the effort was called off after about five hours. A joint city and Coast Guard team then deployed a 50-metre-long, 6.8-metre-high net. In one attempt, officials pushed the shark to within about 100 metres of the canal exit. The following day it simply crossed the net and moved further into the canal.

Authorities have now stopped trying. Instead, they are monitoring the animal and waiting for it to leave on its own. The National Institute of Fisheries Science checks on it daily. A wound on its snout, probably from scraping against something hard, has not worsened. The canal’s salinity is close to that of the open sea, with no freshwater flowing in, and there is plenty of prey, including mullet and horse mackerel. Basically, it has found a quiet room with a well-stocked fridge.

There is a clock ticking, though. The water is currently around 22 °C, and experts quoted by the Asia Business Daily say the shark may struggle if it drops to about 18 °C. Officials hope that as autumn cools the canal, Bukangi will decide to head back out to warmer water. A city official told Korea JoongAng Daily earlier in October that they believed the water would stay warm enough through the end of the month.

Meanwhile, Busan has embraced its accidental celebrity. During the Chuseok holiday in late September, daily visits averaged more than 120,000. By the one-month mark, more than 1.5 million people had visited, which the Asia Business Daily points out is roughly the entire regular-season attendance of the Lotte Giants baseball team’s 71 home games last year. Access to the canal is now closed overnight, from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

Local businesses have noticed. Kang Gi-seong, who runs the Ediya Coffee branch inside the park, donated one million won to the district’s hometown donation programme, saying he wanted to give some of the unexpected earnings back to the community.

There is also a more practical side effect: on 13 October the city said it would study ways to keep sharks away from its beaches, including possibly classifying sharks as harmful marine life so that protective nets can be installed. For now, though, Bukangi keeps doing laps.

items.title: Portugal tem uma segunda língua oficial, e não é o português de outra região
items.snippet: O mirandês, falado em Miranda do Douro, descende do antigo leonês e é reconhecido por lei desde 1999. Até já tem Astérix e Os Lusíadas.
body: Muita gente não sabe, mas o português não é a única língua reconhecida oficialmente em Portugal. Desde 1999, a Lei n.º 7/99 reconhece o mirandês, falado na Terra de Miranda, em torno de Miranda do Douro e de parte de Vimioso, no nordeste transmontano.
O mirandês não é um dialeto do português. Pertence ao grupo asturo-leonês e descende do antigo leonês, a língua do Reino de Leão. Tem fonologia, gramática e vocabulário próprios.

Um inquérito da Universidade de Vigo, de 2020, estimou cerca de 3500 falantes, e a UNESCO considera-o definitivamente em perigo. Mas a língua tem resistido com obras traduzidas por Amadeu Ferreira, de Astérix a Os Lusíadas.
more: Na raia transmontana, encostada a Espanha, fala-se há séculos uma língua que soa familiar e estranha ao mesmo tempo para quem fala português. O mirandês é falado na chamada Terra de Miranda, em Miranda do Douro e na parte oriental de Vimioso, a que os falantes chamam Bumioso.

A sua origem está a norte e a leste. O mirandês descende do antigo leonês, a língua falada no Reino de Leão na Idade Média, e pertence à família asturo-leonesa, a mesma de variedades ainda faladas nas Astúrias e em Leão, em Espanha. Curiosamente, conservou arcaísmos que as variedades espanholas já perderam, o que faz dele uma espécie de cápsula do tempo linguística.

O reconhecimento oficial chegou em 1999, com a Lei n.º 7/99, que lhe deu estatuto de língua co-oficial com o português para assuntos locais em Miranda do Douro. No mesmo ano foi aprovada a primeira ortografia oficial, revista em 2000, baseada sobretudo na ortografia portuguesa, com ajustes para os sons próprios do mirandês. Em 2001 a língua foi reconhecida pelo European Bureau for Lesser-Used Languages.
Há três variedades principais: o raiano, junto à fronteira, o central e o sendinês, da zona de Sendim.

Uma figura central na vida recente da língua foi Amadeu Ferreira, que traduziu para mirandês o primeiro álbum do Astérix, em 2005, e Os Lusíadas de Camões, em 2009. Seguiram-se os Evangelhos, em 2011, e a Bíblia completa, em 2013. Ter Astérix e Camões na mesma língua minoritária é talvez a melhor prova de que uma língua está viva: serve tanto para a epopeia como para a banda desenhada.

Além do reconhecimento legal, a língua tem também uma presença cultural própria, com tradução literária, estudos e uma comunidade que se esforça por a manter viva. O próprio facto de ter uma ortografia oficial desde 1999 permitiu que passasse a ser escrita de forma consistente, o que é essencial para o ensino e para a publicação de livros.

Ainda assim, a situação é frágil. Os números de falantes variam muito conforme a fonte: um inquérito da Universidade de Vigo, de 2020, apontou para cerca de 3500 falantes, enquanto outras estimativas falam de 1000 a 1500 utilizadores regulares. O mesmo estudo encontrou uma quebra acentuada no uso entre os mais novos. A UNESCO classifica o mirandês como definitivamente em perigo, e a Wikipédia nota que Portugal ainda não ratificou a Carta Europeia das Línguas Regionais ou Minoritárias.
Da próxima vez que se passar por Miranda do Douro, vale a pena prestar atenção e, se houver sorte, ouvir uma conversa em mirandês num café. É uma das heranças mais discretas e mais preciosas do país.

items.title: A Biblioteca Joanina, em Coimbra, tem morcegos a proteger os livros todas as noites
items.snippet: Uma colónia de morcegos vive dentro da biblioteca barroca e come os insetos que estragariam os livros. De manhã, limpa-se o guano.
body: A Biblioteca Joanina, no coração da Universidade de Coimbra, é uma das bibliotecas mais bonitas do mundo. Foi construída entre 1717 e 1728 por ordem de D. João V e recebeu os primeiros livros em 1750.

Tem um segredo que encanta qualquer visitante: dentro dela vive uma colónia de morcegos. À noite, saem e comem os insetos que poderiam roer o papel dos livros antigos. É um dos dois casos conhecidos no mundo; o outro é a biblioteca do Palácio de Mafra.
Em troca, há trabalho para os funcionários: todas as noites tapam as mesas com mantas de couro e, de manhã, limpam os excrementos dos morcegos.
more: A Biblioteca Joanina deve o nome a D. João V, o rei que mandou começar a obra em 1717, no início do Iluminismo. O arquiteto foi João Carvalho Ferreira e a construção ficou pronta em 1728. Na altura chamava-se Casa da Livraria e só recebeu os primeiros livros em 1750. Hoje é Monumento Nacional e faz parte da Universidade de Coimbra.

Lá dentro, o barroco está em todo o lado. O edifício tem três pisos e três grandes salas separadas por arcos decorados. As paredes estão forradas com estantes de dois andares em madeiras exóticas douradas ou pintadas, sobretudo do Brasil, com motivos chineses. Os tetos foram pintados pelos artistas lisboetas Simões Ribeiro e Vicente Nunes, e o grande retrato de D. João V é de Domenico Duprà, de 1725. Sobre a entrada estão as armas nacionais.

O acervo tem dezenas de milhares de volumes dos séculos XVI a XVIII, sobre medicina, geografia, história, ciência, direito, filosofia e teologia. A Wikipédia dá números diferentes conforme a secção, de mais de 70 mil a cerca de 250 mil volumes, por isso o número exato fica em aberto. Os livros podem ser consultados mediante pedido justificado.

A conservação foi pensada desde o início. O edifício funciona quase como um cofre: as paredes exteriores têm cerca de 2,11 metros de espessura, o que mantém o interior estável ao longo do ano. Uma porta de teca ajuda a manter a temperatura entre 18 e 20 graus e a humidade perto dos 60%. A estrutura é de carvalho, uma madeira densa cujo cheiro afasta os insetos que comem papel.

E depois há os morcegos. Uma colónia vive dentro da biblioteca e, durante a noite, alimenta-se dos insetos que poderiam danificar os livros. É um controlo de pragas totalmente natural. A Joanina é uma de apenas duas bibliotecas no mundo com este sistema; a outra é a do Palácio Nacional de Mafra, também ela barroca e também ligada a D. João V.

Claro que ter morcegos como guardas tem custos. Todas as noites, os funcionários cobrem as credências e mesas com mantas de couro, para as proteger. De manhã, a biblioteca é limpa do guano deixado pelos pequenos inquilinos.

É uma daquelas histórias que parecem inventadas para turistas, mas que é verdadeira e ao mesmo tempo muito portuguesa: uma solução engenhosa, antiga e discreta, que continua a funcionar sem grandes alaridos. Da próxima vez que se visitar Coimbra, vale a pena lembrar que aquela sala dourada tem turno da noite.

items.title: A aliança entre Portugal e Inglaterra tem mais de 650 anos e ainda está em vigor
items.snippet: Selada em 1373 e em 1386 com o Tratado de Windsor, é a mais antiga aliança diplomática ainda ativa. Em 1927 os britânicos pensaram acabar com ela, mas não sabiam como.
body: A aliança luso-britânica é muitas vezes descrita como a mais antiga aliança do mundo ainda em vigor. Os laços vêm de 1294, foram renovados pelo Tratado de Tagilde, em 1372, e pelo tratado anglo-português de 1373, e ficaram selados com o Tratado de Windsor, em 1386.
Um ano depois, Filipa de Lencastre, filha de João de Gaunt, casou com D. João I. Os filhos do casal ficaram conhecidos como a Ínclita Geração, incluindo o Infante D. Henrique.

A aliança foi invocada nas Invasões Francesas, nas duas guerras mundiais e até na Guerra das Malvinas. E há uma curiosidade deliciosa: em 1927, o governo britânico estudou se valia a pena mantê-la e descobriu que o tratado não tinha forma de ser dissolvido.
more: Há alianças que duram uma guerra. Esta já atravessou mais de seis séculos. A ligação entre Portugal e Inglaterra tem raízes em 1294, foi renovada pelo Tratado de Tagilde, em 1372, e pelo tratado anglo-português de 1373, e foi selada pelo Tratado de Windsor, em 1386. É por isso apresentada como a mais antiga aliança ainda em vigor por acordo político bilateral.

Como era costume na época, a política resolveu-se também com um casamento. Em 1387, Filipa de Lencastre, filha de João de Gaunt, duque de Lencastre, casou com D. João I de Portugal. Desse casamento nasceram os príncipes que a história portuguesa chama Ínclita Geração, entre os quais o Infante D. Henrique, figura central dos Descobrimentos.

Ao longo dos séculos, a aliança foi chamada várias vezes à ação. Durante a Guerra Peninsular, contra Napoleão, a ajuda britânica foi decisiva para restaurar a independência portuguesa, e a família real partiu para o Brasil escoltada pela marinha britânica. Na Primeira Guerra Mundial, tropas portuguesas combateram na Frente Ocidental ao lado dos Aliados.

Na Segunda Guerra Mundial, Portugal manteve-se oficialmente neutro, mas a aliança não ficou na gaveta. Em 1940 apoiou o uso da Madeira na evacuação de civis de Gibraltar, e em 1943 Portugal concedeu ao Reino Unido facilidades navais e aéreas nos Açores, que acabaram também por ser usadas pelos Estados Unidos. Já em 1982, durante a Guerra das Malvinas, Portugal voltou a oferecer instalações nos Açores à Royal Navy.

A curiosidade mais saborosa vem de 1927. Nesse ano, o governo britânico fez uma revisão para perceber se a aliança ainda valia a pena. Os consultores jurídicos repararam num pormenor: o tratado não tinha qualquer mecanismo de dissolução. Sem uma maneira prevista de acabar com ela, a Grã-Bretanha decidiu mantê-la. É talvez a única aliança que sobreviveu, em parte, por ninguém saber como a terminar.

Hoje, os dois países são também membros da NATO, o que torna a velha aliança mais simbólica do que operacional. Mas os símbolos contam. Em 2022, uma declaração conjunta assinalou os 650 anos do Tratado de Tagilde, e em 2023 os dois países comemoraram os 650 anos do tratado de 1373.
Ao longo destes séculos, a relação nem sempre foi pacífica nem equilibrada, mas a estrutura formal manteve-se, renovada e lembrada sempre que um dos lados precisou do outro.

Para quem gosta de história, é uma ideia curiosa: quando D. João I e Filipa de Lencastre casaram, ainda faltava mais de um século para Colombo chegar à América. E o acordo que os juntou continua formalmente de pé.

items.title: Encontrado no Pejão um inseto com 298 milhões de anos, mais velho que os dinossauros
items.snippet: Investigadoras da Universidade do Porto descreveram uma ninfa fóssil de uma espécie nunca vista, achada numa antiga mina de carvão.
body: Uma equipa da Faculdade de Ciências da Universidade do Porto anunciou a descoberta de uma ninfa de inseto fossilizada com cerca de 298 milhões de anos. Foi encontrada na mina da Paraduça, no Pejão, no distrito de Aveiro, em xistos do Carbonífero Superior.

A ninfa tem cerca de 10 milímetros, oito segmentos visíveis e restos das patas. Parece-se com a ninfa de uma libélula atual. As patas traseiras robustas e o abdómen volumoso sugerem que viveria na água. Não corresponde a nenhuma ninfa conhecida desta época, por isso deverá ser uma espécie nova.
O fóssil foi encontrado por Sara Silva, doutorada em Geociências, e identificado com a ajuda de Helena Couto. O estudo foi publicado na revista Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie.
more: A descoberta foi anunciada a 14 de outubro, mas o artigo científico já tinha sido publicado a 15 de setembro na revista alemã Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie. Além de Sara Silva e de Helena Couto, professora aposentada da FCUP e investigadora do Instituto de Ciências da Terra, assinam o trabalho André Nel, do Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, em Paris, e Torsten Wappler, da Universidade de Bona.

A rocha veio da mina da Paraduça, no Pejão, uma exploração de carvão a céu aberto na Bacia Carbonífera do Douro. Segundo o Observador, a mina fica no concelho de Vale de Cambra, embora outras notícias a situem noutros concelhos do distrito de Aveiro. Sara Silva recolheu a amostra durante os trabalhos de extração, nos xistos do Carbonífero Superior, o período que vai de cerca de 323 a 298 milhões de anos atrás. Para pôr isto em perspetiva: os primeiros dinossauros só apareceriam dezenas de milhões de anos depois.

O fóssil é pequeno, com cerca de um centímetro, mas conta muito. Vêem-se fragmentos das patas, oito segmentos do corpo e cercos curtos, os pequenos apêndices na ponta do abdómen. A ausência de asas desenvolvidas indica que se trata de um indivíduo jovem. A forma lembra as ninfas das libélulas modernas, e as patas traseiras grandes e fortes, juntamente com o abdómen volumoso, levam os investigadores a sugerir um modo de vida aquático.

Classificar o animal é difícil. Helena Couto sublinhou que as ninfas de insetos do Carbonífero são raras e complicadas de atribuir a grupos específicos. A equipa coloca-a, de forma provisória, perto da ordem extinta Paoliida, embora a posição das patas lembre também os plecópteros, os insetos conhecidos em inglês como stoneflies. O que parece claro é que não corresponde a nenhuma ninfa paleozoica conhecida, o que aponta para uma espécie ainda não descrita.

A Bacia Carbonífera do Douro é um dos principais registos continentais deste período em Portugal. As minas de carvão do Pejão, que durante décadas alimentaram a indústria, guardam assim também um arquivo de florestas e de pequenos animais que viveram numa paisagem muito diferente da atual.

Também há aqui uma lição sobre ciência e acaso. O fóssil não foi encontrado numa grande escavação planeada, mas numa amostra recolhida durante trabalhos numa mina a céu aberto, e foi preciso o olhar treinado de uma geocientista para perceber que aquela pequena mancha na rocha era um animal.

Os investigadores esperam agora encontrar um exemplar ainda mais bem preservado, que permita ver as estruturas da cabeça e as fases iniciais do desenvolvimento das asas. Até lá, este pequeno inseto de um centímetro já conseguiu algo notável: tornar-se notícia quase 300 milhões de anos depois de ter vivido.

items.title: O Porto foi eleito a cidade mais acolhedora da Europa, com Lisboa logo atrás
items.snippet: Nos prémios dos leitores da Condé Nast Traveller, o Porto ficou em 1.º na Europa e em 2.º no mundo, só atrás de Melbourne.
body: Os leitores da revista de viagens Condé Nast Traveller elegeram o Porto como a cidade mais acolhedora da Europa nos Readers’ Choice Awards 2026. A cidade teve 98,33 pontos e ficou em segundo lugar no mundo, apenas 0,19 pontos atrás de Melbourne, na Austrália.
Lisboa ficou logo a seguir no ranking europeu, com 97,60 pontos, à frente de Amesterdão, Estocolmo e Valeta.

A categoria avalia a hospitalidade e a disponibilidade dos habitantes para ajudar quem visita, por exemplo a encontrar o metro ou a perceber a ementa de um restaurante. Noutra lista dos mesmos prémios, a das melhores cidades da Europa, o Porto ficou em sétimo lugar.
more: Os Readers’ Choice Awards da Condé Nast Traveller estão na 29.ª edição e baseiam-se nas avaliações dos próprios leitores sobre os destinos que visitaram. A votação deste ano decorreu entre 1 de abril e 30 de junho de 2026 e os resultados foram divulgados a 6 de outubro. A New in Porto, da NiT, deu a notícia a 13 de outubro com um título que diz tudo: “Mas havia dúvidas?”

Na categoria de cidades mais acolhedoras, o Porto somou 98,33 pontos, o que lhe valeu o primeiro lugar europeu e o segundo lugar mundial. Melbourne, na Austrália, ficou à frente por uma margem mínima, com 98,52 pontos. Segundo a explicação da revista citada pela NiT, as pontuações correspondem aos níveis médios de satisfação dos participantes.

O pódio europeu é quase todo português. Depois do Porto, aparece Lisboa com 97,60 pontos, seguida de Amesterdão, com 97,50, Estocolmo, com 96,67, e Valeta, capital de Malta, com 95. Duas cidades portuguesas nos dois primeiros lugares de uma votação sobre simpatia é o tipo de resultado que confirma aquilo que muitos turistas comentam à saída do país.

O que é que conta, afinal, para ser acolhedor? A revista olha para a hospitalidade e para a disponibilidade dos residentes para ajudar quem chega. Os exemplos dados são muito concretos: alguém que explica como chegar ao metro, ou que ajuda a decifrar a ementa de um restaurante. Quem já viu um portuense a apontar o caminho com três desvios e uma recomendação de francesinha pelo meio percebe a pontuação.

O Porto apareceu também noutra lista dos mesmos prémios, a das melhores cidades da Europa, onde ficou em sétimo lugar, com 92,78 pontos, numa tabela liderada por Paris. Aí, a revista destacou o centro histórico classificado pela UNESCO, a gastronomia, a arte urbana, os azulejos, a proximidade das praias e, claro, o vinho do Porto.

Convém lembrar que estes rankings não são estudos científicos: refletem a opinião de quem respondeu à votação. Ainda assim, a diferença mínima para Melbourne e a presença de Lisboa logo a seguir mostram que a imagem de Portugal como um país que recebe bem não é apenas uma frase de brochura turística.

A notícia foi recebida com satisfação na cidade, e a Câmara do Porto também a divulgou. Resta o lado menos óbvio destes prémios: ser acolhedor depende das pessoas, não dos monumentos. É um elogio aos portuenses, aos lisboetas e a quem trabalha todos os dias com quem chega de fora, mesmo nas semanas em que a cidade parece ter mais visitantes do que ruas.

items.title: Where did millions of tons of World War II military hardware actually go?
items.snippet: From French tanks reused by German rear guards to Nazi Messerschmitts forming Israel's first air force, post-WWII weapons had bizarrely long second lives.
body: Humanity has rarely produced as much physical machinery as it did during the Second World War. But once the dust settled across Europe and Asia, the sheer mountain of tanks, trucks, and rifles didn't just vanish into scrap heaps.

Early in the war, captured hardware had already been recycled extensively out of sheer necessity. By 1945, modern equipment held by the US and the USSR was used to rearm emerging Cold War allies, while vast stockpiles were sold off to neutral nations. In fact, many South American countries relied on their WWII acquisitions well into the 1980s, with Chile keeping the Sherman Firefly as its main battle tank until the end of the Cold War.

Surplus gear often embarked on strange geopolitical journeys: captured German panzers were sold to Syria, while early Israeli forces secretly acquired Messerschmitt Bf 109 fighters through Czechoslovakia.
more: A detailed breakdown on r/AskHistorians revealed just how fluidly equipment changed hands before and after 1945. Contrary to the myth of a fully motorized German force, fewer than 10% of German divisions were motorized in 1939–1940. Captured French, Belgian, and Dutch trucks became the primary backbone that allowed Germany to mechanize enough units to invade the Soviet Union.

However, operating captured foreign machinery was a logistical nightmare. Incompatible tooling, unstandardized parts, and metric-versus-imperial differences made field maintenance brutal. By 1944, the 17th SS-Panzergrenadier-Division was driving transport trucks sourced from four or five distinct nations, while British paratroopers dropping into Arnhem were astonished to take fire from captured Lee-Enfield rifles and Bren guns originally abandoned at Dunkirk four years earlier.

Post-war transfers created equally bizarre alignments. When France fought in Indochina between 1946 and 1950, American resistance to French colonial policy meant the French military had to scrape together abandoned pre-war Japanese armor and planes, along with captured German Sd.Kfz. half-tracks and British Bren Carriers. Elite French para-commandos heavily favored the German MP-40 submachine gun.

That calculus shifted abruptly in 1950 with the outbreak of the Korean War. Seeing France as a front against Asian communism, Washington opened discounted Pacific stockpiles in the Philippines, flooding Indochina with surplus American gear and retiring the improvised international menagerie for good.

items.title: Chuck Lorre escaped Scientology without harassment because he was broke
items.snippet: While high-profile defectors faced intense surveillance and intimidation, the sitcom creator slipped away unnoticed because he had empty pockets.
body: Former members of the Church of Scientology have long shared harrowing stories about being stalked, harassed, and surveilled under the group's aggressive policies against defectors. Yet mega-producer Chuck Lorre managed an almost frictionless exit.

In his memoir 'Sitcom: A Memoir', the creator behind hits like 'The Big Bang Theory' and 'Two and a Half Men' explained that he spent a decade in the church during his early days as a struggling musician. He had even signed a one-billion-year employment contract with its Sea Org.

When Lorre and his wife finally decided to walk away after losing faith in the organization's promises, they experienced no stalking. Lorre attributes this directly to his lack of wealth: 'Turns out this is only true if the departing thetans have any money. We were so broke, no one noticed we were gone.'
more: Lorre turned to Scientology during a vulnerable, difficult chapter of his life, hoping it would deliver miraculous changes. When his father fell gravely ill, Lorre genuinely believed Scientology practices could heal him, and he maintained that faith even as he developed severe ulcerative colitis himself.

Eventually, Lorre and his then-wife Paula Smith realized the promised blessings were not materializing. While leaving cost them all their church friends overnight, they dodged the retaliatory campaigns common to high-profile defectors chronicled in documentaries like 'Going Clear'.

For decades, Lorre kept his past involvement quiet—not out of fear, but simple embarrassment. As he acknowledged to Variety, he spent an entire decade wrapped up in the belief system, but chose to view it as an unfortunate stepping stone on the road to his current career.
With nearly a billion years technically left on his old Sea Org contract, Lorre joked about finally addressing the topic in print: 'If there’s a knock at the door, I’ll let you know.'

items.title: TIL an imposing Soviet iron fountain survived an earthquake that leveled a city
items.snippet: In Gyumri, Armenia, an architect's brutalist metal fountain stood its ground while the neighborhood around it collapsed to dust.
body: In 1982, architect Artur Tarkhanyan erected an enormous, futuristic iron fountain along a grand Soviet boulevard in Gyumri, Armenia.

Just six years later, a catastrophic earthquake struck in 1988, devastating the city and flattening nearly every surrounding apartment block and building into rubble. Yet the heavy iron fountain stubbornly remained upright amid the devastation.
Although its structural shell survived, the quake obliterated the underlying plumbing system. The monumental sculpture has stood bone-dry ever since, an enduring relic of late-Soviet architecture.
more: Visitors arriving in late winter describe a haunting post-Soviet tableau: cracked concrete slabs that once formed wide urban promenades, overgrown bushes, and decaying apartment blocks that survived the disaster or were left half-abandoned.

Artur Tarkhanyan was known for his modernist and brutalist civic designs in Soviet Armenia. The fountain's rugged iron framework was sturdy enough to weather forces that brought down multi-story residential towers, saving the abstract structure even as the vibrant civic square around it vanished.
Today, the monument serves as an unintentional memorial to the 1988 disaster. It never sprayed water again, standing completely silent and imposing against the gray winter skies of Gyumri.

items.title: Maxon Releases Cinema 4D 2027.0
items.snippet: Cinema 4D 2027.0 is out, featuring a dedicated MoGraph scattering tool, secondary foam and spray mechanics, and expanded Scene Nodes control.
body: Maxon has officially rolled out Cinema 4D 2027.0, introducing a collection of toolset overhauls geared toward layout artists and motion designers. The headliner is a dedicated scattering engine fully integrated into MoGraph, long requested as an alternative to clunky Cloner-and-Field workarounds.

The new Scatter Generator and Scatter Tag let you populate environments with foliage, rocks, or debris across surfaces, splines, or UV maps, complete with clustering, random variation, and proximity rules. Complementing it are secondary Liquid FX tools that inject spray, foam, and bubble particles directly into existing liquid simulations.

Under the hood, Cinema 4D expands its Scene Nodes system, bundles Redshift 2027.0 with a new procedural Fur engine, and adds direct clipboard support to paste cameras, nulls, and primitives straight into Maxon's Autograph app.
more: For artists routinely tasked with populating wide natural terrains or dense architectural scenes, the new MoGraph Scatter Generator simplifies workflows substantially. Rather than forcing complex hierarchy stacks with traditional Cloner objects, users can scatter assets across geometry based on scatter or density texture maps, procedural filters, or proximity boundaries. The accompanying Scatter Tag provides granular overrides directly on individual objects to dial in variations in scale, color, and cluster density.

Liquid simulations receive a major upgrade via dedicated Liquid FX mechanics designed to fix previous scale limitations. The Liquid FX Emitter watches particle behavior across surfaces, generating secondary spray and foam particles at fast-moving, high-curvature crests, or spawning internal bubbles in pockets of trapped air. An accompanying Modifier turns existing fluid particles directly into secondary elements, making setups like effervescent liquids or carbonated drinks far more practical.

Parametric setups also gain deeper node connectivity. The new Scene Nodes Field and Scene Nodes Effector objects let artists construct custom mathematical fields from scratch, which Maxon describes as significantly more efficient than Python Fields. Notably, these node setups hook into the MCP Server introduced in version 2026.4, opening the door for external AI tools like Claude Desktop to trigger and adjust node behaviors programmatically.

On the workflow side, Maxon expanded CAD import pipelines to support formats like 3MF, 3DXML, and IFC, alongside proprietary file types from Solid Edge, NX, Inventor, and PTC Creo. Viewport improvements include random color assignment for objects, HUD hotkey hints, and tag grouping.

Cinema 4D 2027.0 is available on Windows 11 and macOS 15.0+ under Maxon's subscription model at $109 per month or $839 annually. It ships with Redshift 2027.0, which introduces ACES 2 color space management and updates to the Redshift Live real-time preview.

items.title: Chris Ullens Animates Tiny Artisans for Diptyque
items.snippet: Director Chris Ullens shrinks down the luxury candlemaking process into a tactile stop-motion short for Diptyque's Médicis wax vase.
body: Director Chris Ullens has released a detailed stop-motion film for French perfumer Diptyque, visualizing the creation of their Médicis wax vase. The piece follows a miniature crew of apron-wearing craftsmen working along miniature curved benches and softly lit architectural arches.

To highlight the physical artistry behind the object, Ullens juxtaposes the tiny workers' deliberate motions against full-sized candles on the workbench. The warm, restrained color palette emphasizes tactile textures rather than flashy visual effects.

The project brought together character design by Connor Chung, 3D rigging by Gary Mellor, 3D printing by Aldo Camilleri, and hand painting by Rosie Tonkin, alongside practical set design shot on physical stages.
more: In commercial motion work, high-end practical craft continues to stand apart from digital workflows. Commissioned by Diptyque, Chris Ullens conceived, directed, and personally animated the film to turn the industrial process of wax manufacturing into something intimate and handmade.

The production pipeline relied heavily on digital fabrication merged with traditional finishing. Connor Chung developed the stylized character designs, which Gary Mellor then rigged in 3D to plan articulable movements. Aldo Camilleri handled the miniature 3D printing of the figures, before Rosie Tonkin painstakingly cleaned and painted each miniature puppet by hand.

Lighting and staging played a critical role in selling the scale. Cinematographer Jamie Durand illuminated the curved miniature arches to evoke an old-world workshop, while art director Ben Cote grounded the workspace with realistic miniature tools, molds, and benches. A real, full-scale candle sits adjacent to the tiny workstations, providing an immediate visual anchor for scale.

Alongside the main film, Ullens shared a behind-the-scenes making-of video highlighting the meticulous frame-by-frame puppet manipulation and the practical sets required to capture the liquid wax pours in camera. Sound design and original score were provided by Audio’s Most Valuable.

items.title: Anna Huijun Wang’s OROBORO Collapses Dimensional Boundaries
items.snippet: From a single cel-drawn eye to full 3D and back again, Anna Huijun Wang's graduation film explores the weight of modern digital identity.
body: Created as her thesis project at USC’s Hench Division of Animation & Digital Arts, director Anna Huijun Wang’s short film OROBORO charts a surreal visual evolution of identity. The piece starts with a solitary hand-drawn eye that morphs outward into 2D graphic motion design.

As the character absorbs digital noise, products, and online media, she grows limbs, structure, and depth, eventually graduating into complete 3D space. The visual density mirrors information overload until the structure glitches, sheds its dimensions, and collapses back to its simple beginning.
Featuring graphic design work by Matthew Sorgie and sound by Penrose Audio, the film uses fluid transitions between animation mediums as emotional states rather than mere stylistic experiments.
more: In OROBORO, medium shifts function as the core narrative driver. The protagonist's physical expansion tracks the psychological burden of identity building in a media-saturated environment. Traditional cel animation represents an embryonic, singular consciousness that expands rapidly as outside cultural influences take hold.

As the visual pacing accelerates, flat vector motion graphics take over to represent structured, commercialized interaction. Wang layers modern visual tropes—social media graphics, branded interfaces, and geometric limbs—before transitioning into shaded 3D dimensionality as the protagonist reaches peak complexity.

The narrative arc turns when the weight of accumulating identity becomes unsustainable. The character begins to suffer visual artifacts, tearing through dimensional layers and shedding polygons to return to flat space, ultimately resolving back to the hand-drawn eye from the opening frame.

The film highlights a smooth blending of production methods, utilizing Matthew Sorgie’s sharp graphic design to bridge the gap between organic hand-drawn sequences and structured 3D spaces. Penrose Audio provided the music and sound design, building dynamic shifts in audio fidelity that mirror the visuals as they morph from clean textures to distorted digital noise.

items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein Lands in ComfyUI as a 5.6B Open Model
items.snippet: Black Forest Labs has dropped FLUX 3 Image Klein, bringing native 4K output, bounding-box composition control, and 8-second generation to consumer GPUs.
body: Black Forest Labs has released FLUX 3 Image Klein, a compact 5.6-billion-parameter open-weights image model now integrated directly into ComfyUI.
